title: How Redwood Materials uses AI to sort batteries for recycling at scale
excerpt: Tesla cofounder JB Straubel's Redwood Materials says its AI-powered sorting line identifies old batteries with more than 98% accuracy.
content_html:
Redwood Materials found a very practical use for AI: Sorting old batteries

By Alistair Barr

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

Author of the AI Insider newsletter

2026-11-21T15:28:01.255Z

Recycling batteries sounds like a great idea. Until you realize someone has to sort through mountains of them first.

It's a tricky job. Batteries come in all shapes and sizes, with different chemical ingredients. Mixing up the wrong ones can make recycling less efficient and more expensive.

Enter AI.

Redwood Materials, the battery recycling startup founded by Tesla cofounder JB Straubel, has built an automated sorting system that can identify batteries with more than 98% accuracy, according to the company.

Here's how it works.

Old batteries arrive in a jumble of boxes and bins. Machines separate them into a single-file line. Each battery then passes through a tunnel equipped with cameras and sensors that examine its label, shape, and weight.

AI figures out what kind of battery it is and sends it to the right place for recycling. Redwood developed an AI model for this, trained on the company's voluminous battery data, and it runs on a cluster of GPUs on site.

The system was built in just a few months and can handle several tons of batteries an hour.

Why does this matter?

Redwood wants to recover valuable materials such as lithium, nickel, and cobalt, rather than relying so heavily on mining and imports.

This is a neat example of AI tackling a messy, unglamorous industrial problem. And potentially making American manufacturing more competitive.
